newsitem.title: INDIA: Human rights key agenda for security forces - India.
newsitem.headline: Human rights key agenda for security forces - India.

text.p: Indian security forces, periodically accused of human rights abuses in insurgency-hit areas, are being trained to stop such excesses as a top priority, the Home (Interior) Ministry said on Friday.

The ministry annual report praised recent efforts by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) to promote an understanding of human rights laws by the paramilitary, police and army personnel.
"These efforts have resulted in a greater degree of responsibility and sensitisation on the part of the security forces," the report for the 1996/97 year ended on March 31 said.

On their part, the security forces were grappling with an upsurge of left-wing violence in some states and continued attacks by separatist militants, particularly in four remote northeastern states and Kashmir, the report said.
"The government continued to follow a multi-pronged strategy on human rights matters," said the report, covering a period when the ministry was headed by three ministers with distinct ideologies.

The home ministers were Shankarrao Chavan of the centrist Congress party, Murli Manohar Joshi of the right-wing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party and Inderjit Gupta of the Communist Party of India, a member of the ruling United Front alliance.
The measures included "strict enforcement of constitutional and legal safeguards, stern action against officials found guilty of human rights violations".
India set up the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) in 1993 to monitor and report on rights excesses, including army operations in the northern state of Jammu and Kashmir.
The report said regional versions of the NHRC were now being set up by state governments, which are primarily responsible for law and order.

Three one-day workshops on human rights were organised by the ICRC in Jammu and Kashmir, where hospitals and police sources say more than 20,000 people have been killed in seven years of separatist violence.

The Border Security Force (BSF) and the Central Reserve Police Force, both paramiliatry groups, and Kashmir police attended these seminars. The BSF held other similar discussions with the ICRC, the report said.

"The government is also committed to signing the U.N. Convention against Torture, and other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, as reflected in its Common Minimum Programme," the report said.
It said greater transparency and awareness of human rights among the security forces and citizens would help in "effectively countering the disinformation campaign of adversaries like Pakistan".

Pakistan accuses Indian forces of raping and killing civilians in divided Kashmir. Islamabad regards these as part of the "core issue of Kashmir" it wants to discuss with India in bilateral talks that began in March after a three-year break.
India controls two-thirds of Kashmir and Pakistan the rest.

Some Kashmiri separatist leaders have hinged their hopes for a breakthrough on Kashmir on new Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral, who was sworn in earlier this week. Some diplomats also expect progress on human rights under Gujral.
The northeastern states of Assam, Tripura, Manipur and Nagaland are the "most affected by insurgent activities of various militant groups", the report said.

The most intractable left-wing militants were the Maoist People's War Group, operating in the Dandakaranya forest region straddling the states of Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh and Orissa.
